summary: Caramulo in fire is an interactive map that tells the story of the July 2026 Tourelhe wildfire in Portugal’s Serra do Caramulo, the country’s largest wildfire that July by area burned. To address the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we developed a guided map experience that uses NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar to reveal where the landscape changed across the fire and how the radar signal varied afterward. Readers can compare observations from before, during and after the fire, explore Sentinel-2 imagery alongside radar data, and compare the radar-derived burn scar with the official perimeter mapped by Portugal’s forest agency, ICNF. The project shows why radar matters for wildfire monitoring: it can help track changes on the ground even when smoke obscures optical imagery.
details:
Caramulo on fire is an interactive map that tells the story of the July 2026 Tourelhe wildfire in Portugal’s Serra do Caramulo. It follows the landscape from before the fire through to the changes visible in later satellite observations. Readers can scroll through six chapters, jump directly to any chapter using the story index, or select their own layers in the final section, “Explore the map”. A comparison slider lets them reveal two views of the same place and examine how the landscape changed.

We use NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar to measure how similar the radar signals were between two satellite passes. This measure is called coherence. We compare a pair of observations spanning the fire with a later pair taken after the fire to identify where coherence dropped during the fire period. We then overlay the radar-derived burn scar on the official perimeter mapped by Portugal’s Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests (ICNF) to see where they agree. NISAR backscatter layers show changes in the strength of the radar return, while Sentinel‑2 true-colour imagery helps readers recognise the landscape.

We used Python to process the satellite data and align the layers on a common geographic grid. We built the web app with React, TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre GL JS and published it on GitHub Pages. The two map views stay aligned as readers move the divider, so the same roads, valleys and slopes line up across observations.

We designed the experience for readers who have never worked with satellite radar. We considered gaps in satellite coverage, the limits of attributing radar changes to fire, and the usability of the map on smaller screens. Our main goal is to show how satellite radar can help monitor a wildfire’s impact even when smoke obscures the ground in optical imagery. By comparing NISAR passes, readers can see where the surface changed across the fire and track how the radar signal evolved on later passes.
